content: The included studies were categorized based on their design: 17 were observational studies, 13 were randomized controlled trials (RCTs), and one was a non-randomized experimental study. The observational studies were referenced as studies 32-39, 42-48, 58, and 59. The RCTs were studies 30, 31, 40, 41, 49-57, 61, and 62, while the non-randomized experimental study was study 60. The geographical distribution of the studies was as follows: nine studies were conducted in Europe, including two each in England (58, 60) and Germany (41, 49), and one each in Denmark (50), Iceland (59), Israel (44), the Netherlands (38), and Sweden (39). Seven studies were conducted in Africa, with one each in the Democratic Republic of Congo (51), Ghana (52), Malawi (31), Senegal (37), Somalia (34), South Africa (33), and Zambia (35). Five studies were conducted in Asia, including two each in Indonesia (32, 46) and Japan (36, 43), and one in Myanmar (45). One study was conducted in Australia (56), and one in Cambodia (57) from the Western Pacific region. Three studies were conducted in North America, including two in the United States (54, 55) and one in Ecuador (30). One study was conducted in Brazil (42) in South America. Additionally, one multi-country study spanned 39 countries across various WHO regions, including Africa, the Americas, Eastern Mediterranean, and Europe (47). The total number of children included in the studies was 278,358, with ages ranging from 6 months to 12 years. However, data were extracted only for children aged 6-23 months. Breastfeeding status was reported in 22 studies (31, 33, 34, 36-46, 49-52, 54, 56-58), while nine studies did not report breastfeeding status (30, 32, 35, 47, 48, 53, 55, 59, 60). Only one study (57) compared breastfeeding status with study outcomes. Regarding the interventions, 13 studies reported the frequency of animal-source food (ASF) consumption, 18 reported the amount, and two reported the variety. The definitions of frequency, amount, and variety varied across studies. For frequency, three studies used 24-hour recall (32, 37, 46), seven used food frequency questionnaires (FFQs) (33, 36, 38, 39, 43-45), one used food survey data (48), one used both 24-hour recall and FFQ (42), and one used structured questionnaires during face-to-face interviews (34). For the amount of ASF consumed, three studies used 24-hour recall of dietary intake (30, 31, 59), three used weekly visits to count empty food packets and record mothers’ reports (40, 51, 54), two used three-day diet records completed by mothers (55, 58), two used 24-hour dietary records before monthly visits (49, 50), and two checked compliance through weekly histories and feeding observations (53, 57). One study used a weighed dietary method (41), and two studies provided discrete amounts of complementary foods to participants (56, 52). One study assessed the amount of ASF using a seven-day weighed food intake (60). For variety, two studies used 24-hour recall to collect data on specific foods consumed (35, 47). The heterogeneity of the data across studies precluded meta-analysis. Various forms of fatty acids were reported, including linoleic acid (LA) in three studies (41, 54, 62), alpha-linoleic acid (ALA) in two studies (41, 62), docosahexaenoic acid (DHA) in three studies (54, 56, 62), and eicosapentaenoic acid (EPA) in two studies (41, 54). One study reported a mix of unprocessed and processed meat (33), one used commercial food (49), and one used processed food (57). A total of 502 studies were excluded. Among the 13 randomized interventional studies, one was rated as high risk of bias (40), nine as moderate risk (30, 31, 41, 50-53, 55, 57), and three as low risk (49, 54, 56). Random allocation was performed in 10 studies (30, 31, 41, 49-52, 54, 56, 57), which were rated as low risk in this domain. Two studies had concerns due to lack of information on allocation concealment (53) or intervention allocation (55), leading to a medium risk of bias. One study did not conceal the allocation sequence (40), resulting in a high risk of bias. Five studies had no deviations from the intended intervention (40, 41, 49, 54, 56), and were rated as low risk of bias. However, eight studies had moderate levels of missing data (40, 41, 49-51, 53, 55, 57), and one study had a high risk of bias due to incomplete outcome measurement (50). Ten studies measured outcomes correctly (30, 31, 40, 41, 49, 53-57), while two had concerns (51, 52). One study did not measure outcomes correctly (50), leading to a high risk of bias. The single non-randomized interventional study (60) had a low to moderate risk of bias overall. Approximately 25% of the sample withdrew before the study's end, raising concerns about internal validity. Additionally, there was no mention of blinding, and the study had moderate to high risk of bias in outcome measurement. For observational studies, 11 did not allow sufficient time to observe an effect, measuring exposure and outcome simultaneously (32, 34-37, 42, 44-48). The remaining studies allotted time to detect an effect (33, 38, 39, 43, 58, 59), presenting a low risk of bias. All 17 observational studies reported different levels of ASF exposure, ensuring a low risk of bias in this domain. However, four studies lacked detailed information on exposure measures (42, 44, 45, 48), leading to a high risk of bias. Four studies assessed exposure more than once over time (32, 33, 58, 59), providing robust findings and a low risk of bias. For 12 studies, exposure was assessed only once (34-39, 42-45, 47, 48), which was not considered a major limitation. Outcome measures were clearly defined, valid, and reliable in 16 studies.
